study.todo.title: What a team does with it
study.todo.body: Before a team reports an AI reading as what participants said, it checks what listening added. Teams can compare models and prompts by what listening added, read beside map size. A later member check can take the AI boxes that are backed by a quote and absent from the endorsed map. Teams compare their results across sites by sharing profiles only, and the interviews stay with each team.

study.reading3.prompt:
You are helping a research team write down the official version of a process.
Describe the typical pathway of a {{role}} in {{domain}}, as official guidance would describe it. You have no interview; use only what is generally known about the process.
Draw it as a map:
- Make one node for each distinct step, service, actor (person or organization) or source of information in the pathway; keep different things in different nodes.
- Put each node in one of these phases: {{phases}}.
- Add a directed edge from one node to another when the official pathway leads from one to the other.
- Every node and edge is part of the official pathway, so mark every node and edge "experienced".
- There is no transcript, so every "quote" must be null.
- Give one word for how the journey typically feels, or null.
Return only JSON in exactly this format. Begin your answer with {{, and write no text before or after the JSON:
{{schema}}
A node's type must be one of the listed types and is never a phase name.
REMINDER: Mark every node and edge "experienced". Every quote is null, because there is no transcript. Use only the phases listed. Reply with only the JSON. Begin your answer with {{

install.title: Install
install.intro: The kit runs on your computer, and it needs Python 3.10 or newer and two models from different families, which can run on your computer, on a server you already use, or through an API. There is nothing to install with pip, because the app runs from its folder.
install.tabs.label: Your operating system
install.step.python.title: Python 3.10 or newer
install.step.python.body.macos: Check the version in Terminal, because the Python that comes with macOS can be older than 3.10; if it is, install Python from python.org or with Homebrew.
install.step.python.body.windows: Check the version in PowerShell, and if py is not found or the version is below 3.10, install Python from python.org; its installer adds the py launcher.
install.step.python.body.linux: Check the version in a terminal, and if it is below 3.10, install a newer python3 from your distribution's packages.
install.step.get.title: Get the code
install.step.get.body: Download the repository as a zip and unzip it, or clone it with git. Then open a terminal in that folder, the one that holds README.md.
install.step.get.body.windows: Download the repository as a zip and unzip it, or clone it with git. Then open PowerShell in that folder, the one that holds README.md.
install.step.start.title: Start the app
install.step.start.where: Run the start command inside the kit folder, the one that holds README.md. If the terminal is open in another folder, move into the kit folder with cd, as in this example for a kit unzipped in Downloads.
install.step.start.where.windows: Run the start command inside the kit folder, the one that holds README.md. If PowerShell is open in another folder, move into the kit folder with cd, as in this example for a kit unzipped in Downloads.
install.step.start.no_module: If the terminal says "No module named second_scribe", it is not in the kit folder. Move into the folder that holds README.md with cd and run the start command again.
install.step.start.body: The terminal prints a link: open it in your browser. The app listens on 127.0.0.1 only, so nothing outside this computer can reach it.
install.step.models.title: Two models from different families
install.step.models.body: The kit needs one model that draws the maps and a judge from another model family. A model never judges its own family's output, so the comparison needs a judge from a different family than the reconstructor.
install.step.models.where: Use the models you already have. In Setup, under "Where the model runs", you enter the address of a model server on your computer or on your network, such as a lab or university server; an institutional gateway or another API that speaks the OpenAI chat format, with its key; or Anthropic's API, with its key. You then tell Setup which family each model is.
install.step.models.reference: As a reference, the study drew the maps with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and judged them with DeepSeek V4 Flash, with Gemma 4 31B as a second judge family. These names are examples and carry no endorsement.
install.step.models.local: To serve models on your own computer, install Ollama from ollama.com, or LM Studio from lmstudio.ai and start its local server. Your own computer is the default, and the authors ran the study only on their own machines. The two commands below pull a small pair of different families that fits on a laptop, for a quick try; choose larger models when your machine can hold them.
install.step.models.one_computer: If you have one computer, the app runs the reconstructor, then asks you to load the judge.
install.step.models.hosted: Send interview text to a hosted API only if your ethics approval allows it. The app then accepts only https addresses and asks you to type the approval it rests on; it keeps that declaration in the app log and prints it on the report.
install.step.no_cloud.title: Keep Ollama on this computer
install.step.no_cloud.body.macos: Set OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD=1 so Ollama turns its cloud models off. For the Ollama app, set it with launchctl and restart the app; if you run Ollama from a terminal, start it with the variable set.
install.step.no_cloud.body.windows: Set OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD=1 so Ollama turns its cloud models off: set it for your user account, then quit Ollama and start it again from the Start menu.
install.step.no_cloud.body.linux: Set OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD=1 so Ollama turns its cloud models off. If Ollama runs as a systemd service, add Environment="OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD=1" under [Service] with systemctl edit, then restart it; if you run it from a terminal, start it with the variable set.

reference.title: Reference
reference.heading: What should each AI map be compared against?
reference.intro: For every transcript the AI draws its own map, and the same model draws the no-interview map. This screen chooses the reference for each transcript: what the AI map is checked against. The AI map is never its own reference.
reference.a.title: A participant-checked map
reference.a.body: The interviewer drew the map with the participant, who endorsed it, and it marks what was missing for them. Gives a full absence check.
reference.a.can: Whether the AI drew as happened a step the participant marked missing, and whether it drew as missing a step that happened.
reference.a.cannot: Anything about steps the participant never put on the map.
reference.a.needs: Needs a paired map that you confirmed in Setup.
reference.b.title: The researcher marks spans
reference.b.body: No participant check. You read the transcript without seeing any AI map and mark the passages where a step happened or was missing. Gives agreement with your reading.
reference.b.can: How far the AI map agrees with your reading of the transcript, and where it drew as happened what you marked missing.
reference.b.cannot: What the person interviewed would say, because results read as agreement between the AI and this researcher's reading; they do not measure distance from the participant and are not a member check.
reference.b.needs: Your coding is hashed and logged before any result opens. Coding time is logged too.
reference.c.title: Automatic checks only
reference.c.body: No participant check and no coding. Works with transcripts only.
reference.c.can: Where a quote the AI used says the opposite of the step it drew.
reference.c.cannot: Which steps were missing for the person: there is nothing to count them against.
reference.c_note: No reference for absences with this reference type.
reference.every_mode_kicker: Runs with every reference type, A, B and C
reference.every_mode_body: For every step, the AI must cite the transcript passage it used. The judge, a model from another family, reads that passage and asks whether it says the step happened or the opposite. A step whose own quote says it did not happen is flagged, whatever the reference.
reference.pooling: Results always carry their reference type. Results from different reference types are never pooled, on screen or in any export.
reference.bulk: Set every transcript with a confirmed map to A
reference.bulk_none: No change: every transcript with a confirmed map is already A.
reference.no_map: A needs a confirmed map for this transcript.
reference.revealed_b: Results have already been shown in this project, so B is no longer open for this transcript.
reference.gate_waiting: Results stay closed until every B coding is locked. Still open: {pids}.
reference.gate_locked: Every B coding in this project is locked.
reference.empty: No transcripts yet. Import transcripts in Setup, then choose a reference for each.

coding.heading: Read and mark
coding.pick_intro: Choose a transcript to read and mark. Results stay closed until every coding here is locked.
coding.none: Nothing to code. No transcript uses reference B, your own reading, so the run needs no coding from you.
coding.not_b: This transcript's reference is not B, so there is nothing to mark here. Choose B for it on the Reference screen.
coding.blind: You code blind. While any B coding in this project is open, the app shows no AI map, no no-interview map and no result, so what you mark is your own reading.
coding.how: Select a passage with the mouse, then give it a step and a mark.
coding.step_hint: Name the step in your own words. Suggestions are only names you used before.
coding.cross_turn: Select words inside one turn. A passage cannot run across two turns.
coding.marks_rule: Every mark points to a verbatim passage. A mark without a passage cannot be saved.
coding.phases_note: Phases come from your project setup, and you name the steps as you read. Results from this coding read as agreement between the AI and this researcher's reading; they do not measure distance from the participant and are not a member check.
coding.time_note: this transcript, logged with your coding
coding.lock_title: Your coding is hashed and logged before any result can open.
coding.confirm_body: After this the marks cannot be changed. The app computes the sha256 of your coding and writes it to the app log. Results open once every B coding in this project is locked.
coding.locked_title: This coding is locked, so it can be read and cannot be changed.

setup.models.filter_hint: Type part of a name or family, such as deepseek. The down arrow moves into the list.
setup.models.other_family: The {other} is {family}. Pick a model from another family.
setup.models.list_empty: Check the address, then list the models.
setup.models.cloud_refused: This model runs in the cloud and off this machine, so it cannot be chosen.

explain.hero.title: What did listening add?
explain.hero.lead: This tool puts three readings of one interview side by side. They are the map the interviewer drew and the participant endorsed, the AI's map from the transcript, and the map the same model draws without the interview. Each reading is measured against the same transcript, and every step is inspectable and re-runnable.

explain.copy_fallback: Selected. Press Ctrl+C, or Cmd+C on a Mac, to copy.
explain.stage_label: How it works, in six scenes
explain.scene.interview: Someone tells their journey in an interview.
explain.scene.endorsed: The interviewer draws the map live, and the participant endorses it.
explain.scene.ai: The AI reads the transcript, alone, and draws its map.
explain.scene.no_interview: The same model draws the no-interview map: domain, role and phases given, no interview.
explain.scene.side_by_side: The three readings side by side, each measured against the same transcript: what did listening add?
explain.scene.own: Run it on your own interviews, on your computer. Labs can pool their profiles, and the interviews stay with each lab.
explain.scene.own_note: The app runs on your computer, and by default nothing leaves your machine. If your ethics approval allows a cloud model, you choose where the text goes, and the app records it.

glossary.instruction_ladder: The instruction ladder is a set of four prompt versions, called rungs, in which only the instruction text changes. Each rung was run once, so every contrast between rungs is descriptive.
glossary.rung1: Rung 1 gives the AI the authors' original draft prompts. It is one of the four rungs of the instruction ladder, and it was run once, like every rung.
glossary.rung2: Rung 2 gives the AI the main run's prompts, the ones behind the study's results. It is one of the four rungs of the instruction ladder, and it was run once, like every rung.
glossary.remedy: The remedy is a prompt version that uses the two prompting strategies of Zhou et al. (2023). The kit calls it rung 3, and it was run once, like every rung.
glossary.placebo: The placebo is a prompt version matched to the remedy in length and format. It was run once, like every rung, so a contrast between the placebo and the remedy is descriptive.
glossary.reconstructor: The reconstructor is the mapping model, the language model that reads a transcript and draws the AI map. The same model also draws the no-interview map.
glossary.judge: The judge is a second language model that labels what each quote reports and decides whether two boxes match. It also decides whether each endorsed step is said in the transcript.
glossary.model_family: Models of one family are built by the same developer, such as two Qwen models. The judge must come from a different family from the reconstructor, because language-model judges favor their own outputs and those of related models.
glossary.second_family: The second judge family is a judge from another model family that labels the same quotes. It shows how much a number depends on one judge.
glossary.temperature: Temperature is the model setting that controls how much its wording varies. At temperature 0 the model chooses its most likely wording at each step, which still does not guarantee identical outputs.
glossary.endorsed_map: The endorsed map is the map the interviewer drew live with the participant during the interview, which the participant later endorsed. Its boxes are steps, services, people and sources of information, placed in the phases of the journey.
glossary.ai_map: The AI map is drawn by a language model from the transcript, after the passages in which the interviewer talked about drawing the map are removed. For every box, the model must cite the participant's exact words.
glossary.no_interview_map: The no-interview map is drawn by the same model without any interview, from the study's topic, a role and the phases only. It describes the official pathway for that role, one map per role.
glossary.no_interview_script: The model's no-interview script holds the steps that appear in at least two of the no-interview drafts the model wrote for a role. The drafts are written at temperature 0.7 so that they differ, and the other family's no-interview script is built in the same way by the judge's family.
glossary.official_pathway: The official pathway is the process as official guidance would describe it. The no-interview map draws it for each role, with no interview.
glossary.mapping_talk: Mapping talk is the passages in which the interviewer talked about drawing the map. They are removed before the AI reads the transcript, so the model works from the conversation alone.
glossary.reference: The reference is the set of endorsed steps that appear in the transcript. Only these steps could in principle be recovered from the transcript, so recall is counted against them.
glossary.wished_for: A box drawn as wished for stands for something the participant needed that never came, a service that should have existed and did not, and the study calls these boxes ideals.
glossary.missing: A box or arrow marked as missing stands for a step the participant needed that did not happen. The analysis reads these boxes as ideals, the steps drawn as wished for.
glossary.flattened: A flattened ideal is a service the participant marked as wished for that the AI map drew as received, while the AI's own quote says that the service did happen.
glossary.member_check: A member check asks participants whether a reading of what they said matches what they meant. In this study, the participant's endorsement of the map drawn during the interview is that check for the endorsed map.
glossary.attested: A box is attested when its quote is found in the participant's own words and the judge's label for that quote agrees with how the box was drawn. A step drawn as received needs a quote that reports something that happened, and a wished-for step needs a quote that reports a wish.
glossary.not_attested: A box is not attested by its own quote when its quote is not found, does not count as evidence, or reports something other than how the box was drawn. Its content may still appear elsewhere in the transcript.
glossary.quote_anchoring: Quote anchoring is the code check that a box's quote appears in the transcript, exactly or with at least 85% of its words in the same order. A box whose quote is not found is left unanchored.
glossary.modality: Modality is what a quote reports, whether something happened, was wished for, was denied, was a hypothetical, or happened to someone else, and the judge labels it for each quote.
glossary.canonical_names: Canonical names are the standard names the judge gives to steps, so that steps worded differently in different maps can be counted as one.
glossary.primary_setting: The primary setting is the stricter of the two main matching rules. Two boxes match when at least 60% of their distinct content words are shared, or when the judge calls the pair the same.
glossary.lenient_setting: The lenient setting is the looser of the two main matching rules. Two boxes match when at least 40% of their distinct content words are shared, or when the judge calls the pair the same or close.
glossary.matcher_setting: A matcher setting is one of eight stored rules for when two boxes match. The eight are word overlap alone at four thresholds, the judge alone in two ways, and the primary and lenient settings, which combine the two.
glossary.lexical_matcher: The lexical matcher pairs two boxes by word overlap alone, the share of their distinct content words that they have in common. It uses no language model, so it pairs almost no paraphrases.
glossary.kept: An endorsed step said in the transcript is kept when some AI box matches it at the primary setting.
glossary.coarsened: An endorsed step said in the transcript is coarsened when an AI box matches it only at the lenient setting. That setting also accepts pairs the judge calls close, where one box is coarser or finer than the other.
glossary.omitted: An endorsed step said in the transcript is omitted when no AI box matches it, at the primary or at the lenient setting.
glossary.recall: Recall is the share of the reference, the endorsed steps said in the transcript, that a map recovers. It is pooled over all maps, as the sum of recovered steps divided by the sum of reference steps.
glossary.attested_recall: Attested recall counts an endorsed step as recovered only when the AI box that matches it is attested by its own quote.
glossary.listening_added: What listening added is the share of endorsed steps that the AI map recovers from the transcript minus the share that the same model recovers with no interview. It would be near zero if the AI had only copied the official pathway.
glossary.precision: Precision is the share of the AI map's boxes that are attested by their own quote and match an endorsed step.
glossary.slant: Slant asks whether the AI map drifts toward the model's no-interview script. The pull is the share of the AI map's boxes found in the model's no-interview script minus the same share for the endorsed map, averaged over maps.
glossary.floor: A floor is the agreement with the endorsed map that is left when a control removes one part of the pipeline, such as the interview, the right person's transcript or the judge.
glossary.lexical_floor: The lexical floor is the recall the AI map reaches when boxes are matched by word overlap alone, without the judge. It shows how much of the recall needs the judge.
glossary.instrument_error: This row shows how far the numbers move when the judge is asked the same questions again, when other labelers read the same quotes, and when a second model draws the maps.
glossary.band: A band is the range of a number across matching settings or labelers, such as from the primary to the lenient setting. It shows how much the number depends on these choices.
glossary.interval: A 95% interval is the range around an estimate from a bootstrap that resamples whole maps. It holds the generated maps and the judge's labels fixed, so it leaves out the variation that would come from asking the models again.
glossary.pooled: A pooled number adds up the counts of all maps before it divides, as in the sum of recovered steps over all maps divided by the sum of reference steps.
glossary.profile: The profile is the one file the kit exports for a run, the distance profile. Each of its rows gives one distance between the AI reading and the endorsed reading, with a value, a band and the steps it rests on.
glossary.ledger: The ledger is the table that sets the two readings of one transcript side by side and counts what each holds that the other lacks.
glossary.pooling: Pooling places the profiles of several labs side by side, within one reference type and one prompt set. The profiles are never combined into one estimate, and the interviews stay with each lab.
glossary.reference_type: The reference type names what each AI map is measured against, the participant-endorsed map (A), the researcher's own blind reading of the transcript (B), or no reference (C). Results of different reference types are never put together.
glossary.hash_chain: A hash chain is a log in which each entry stores a fixed-length fingerprint, a hash, of the entry before it. Any later change to an earlier entry breaks the chain and shows up when the chain is checked.
glossary.chain_head: The head of a chain is the hash of its last entry. A published head lets whoever holds the records detect later edits, but the head alone does not show what the records say.
glossary.declaration_log: The declaration log is a separate hash-chained log of the study's rules and every dated change to them. It shows which rule came before which result.
glossary.gate: The gate is the set of automated checks that a number from the real interviews must pass before it leaves the authors' machines. It refuses results for a single map, splits by interviewer or by role, and any table cell that describes fewer than 10 people.
glossary.app_log: The app log is the project's own hash-chained record of what you imported, removed, confirmed, chose and exported. A change adds a record, and earlier records are never changed.
glossary.speaker_labels: Speaker labels are the marks at the start of each turn of a transcript, such as [P] and [I], or a name followed by a colon. They let the app tell the participant's words from the interviewer's, and only the participant's own words count as evidence.
glossary.pairing: Pairing puts each transcript beside the map drawn in the same interview. The app pairs a transcript and a map when their file names match before the extension, and you confirm the table.
glossary.missing_rule: The missing rule tells the app how your maps mark a box or arrow as missing, for example a red outline or a dashed line. The app reads every map with this rule, and you check what it read before any run.
glossary.model_check: The model check runs the study's instructions on six of the synthetic interviews included with the app, before any of your interviews is read. It checks that this pair of models finds the planted absences.
glossary.opt_in: Allowing a machine on your network lets the app send transcript text to a model server on another computer that you control. The permission is kept in the app log and printed on the run record.
glossary.declaration: A declaration is the record you make before the app may send transcript text to a hosted model. You type the ethics approval it rests on, and the app keeps it in the app log and prints it on the report, the run record and the methods paragraph.
glossary.synthetic: The synthetic interviews are written by the authors about food-truck licensing, with answers known in advance and planted traps. They test the pipeline and say nothing about real interviews.
glossary.trap: A trap is a case planted in a synthetic interview, such as a service the owner only wished for, whose expected outcome is written in advance. The trap table lists the expected and the observed outcome of each trap.
glossary.oracle: The oracle is a stand-in for a perfect AI that answers from the answer key of the synthetic interviews and calls no model. It passes every trap check, so a check that the recorded models do not pass reflects a model's answer.
jobs.server.http: The model server answers with an error (HTTP {status}). Its last answer came {time} ago. The app keeps trying.
jobs.server.timeout: The model server stopped answering in time. Its last answer came {time} ago. The app keeps trying.
jobs.server.no_connection: The app cannot reach the model server. Its last answer came {time} ago. The app keeps trying. Check that the server is running.
jobs.server.transport: The connection to the model server keeps failing. Its last answer came {time} ago. The app keeps trying.
jobs.server.no_reply: The model has not answered for {time}. A slow model can take this long. If the server has stopped, start it again and the app goes on.
